q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: DBE first. Then: what does a 1H signal near 9.6 ppm mean, and why is it a doublet rather than a triplet?
w: DBE = 1. The 1H signal at 9.62 ppm is an aldehyde H; it is a doublet, so the α carbon carries one H. A 6H doublet plus a 1H multiplet (that α-CH) is an isopropyl group. (CH3)2CH–CHO, 2-methylpropanal.
x: Butanal also has a CHO, but its α carbon is CH<sub>2</sub>: the CHO is a triplet, and the spectrum shows 4 signals including a 3H triplet.
2-Butanone has no H above 3 ppm; its signals are a 2H quartet, a 3H singlet and a 3H triplet.
3-Buten-1-ol has vinyl H at 5–6 ppm (3H total), an OCH<sub>2</sub> near 3.7 and an OH; nothing near 9.6 ppm.

q: An ester C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: Two candidate esters have an isopropyl group and an isolated CH<sub>3</sub>. The shift of the septet tells you which side of the ester O the isopropyl is on.
w: 1H septet + 6H doublet = isopropyl; 3H singlet = isolated CH3. The septet is at 4.99 ppm, so the CH is bonded to the ester O (O–CH, strongly deshielded), and the singlet at 2.02 ppm is CH3C=O. Isopropyl acetate, CH3CO2CH(CH3)2.
x: Methyl 2-methylpropanoate has the same three signal types, but its septet (CH next to C=O) is near 2.5 ppm and its singlet (OCH<sub>3</sub>) near 3.7 ppm.
Propyl acetate has a propyl group: an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (4 signals).
Ethyl propanoate shows two ethyl groups (two quartets and two triplets), no septet or singlet.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown, with DEPT results written over the peaks. Which structure is it?
h: Three of the choices give three signals. Use DEPT: which carbon is bonded to O, and is it C, CH or CH<sub>2</sub>?
w: DBE = 0. Three signals for five carbons: a CH2 bonded to O (73.4), a quaternary C (32.6) and CH3 (26.0, three equivalent methyls). (CH3)3C–CH2OH, 2,2-dimethyl-1-propanol, fits.
x: tert-Butyl methyl ether also gives three signals, but its O-bearing carbon is quaternary (≈73, C) and it has an OCH<sub>3</sub> near 49 ppm; it has no CH<sub>2</sub>.
3-Pentanol gives three signals, but its O-bearing carbon is a CH (≈74), with CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> upfield; no quaternary C.
2-Methyl-2-butanol has four kinds of carbon (C–O quaternary, CH<sub>2</sub>, two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>, and the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub>): 4 signals.

q: How can <sup>1</sup>H NMR best distinguish isomers I and II?
c: I shows a 1H vinyl signal near 5.2 ppm; II shows 2H of vinyl signals near 4.7 ppm.
I shows 2H of vinyl signals near 4.7 ppm; II shows a 1H vinyl signal near 5.2 ppm.
Neither has vinyl H, so only <sup>13</sup>C NMR can tell them apart.
They have the same molecular weight, so NMR cannot tell them apart.
h: Count the H on the sp<sup>2</sup> carbons of each isomer and integrate the 4.5–6.5 ppm region.
w: I, 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, has one vinyl H (≈5.2 ppm, 1H). II, 2-methyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3, has a =CH2 group (≈4.7 ppm, 2H). The integration of the vinyl region (1H vs 2H) distinguishes them.
x: The assignments are reversed: the trisubstituted alkene I has one vinyl H, and the 1,1-disubstituted alkene II has two.
Both are alkenes with H on sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, so both show vinyl signals in the 4.5–6.5 ppm region.
Isomers always share a molecular weight; NMR distinguishes them by their different H environments.

q: An aromatic hydrocarbon C8H10 gives five signals in its 13C NMR spectrum. Which compound is it?
h: Draw the symmetry element of each isomer and count the distinct ring carbons, then add the alkyl carbons.
w: 1,3-Dimethylbenzene has a mirror plane through C2 and C5: ring carbons C1/C3, C2, C4/C6 and C5 (4 signals) plus one CH3 signal = 5 signals.
x: 1,2-Dimethylbenzene: ring carbons C1/C2, C3/C6, C4/C5 (3) + CH<sub>3</sub> = 4 signals.
1,4-Dimethylbenzene: ring carbons C1/C4 and the four CH (2) + CH<sub>3</sub> = 3 signals.
Ethylbenzene: four ring signals (ipso, ortho, meta, para) + CH<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub> = 6 signals.

q: An ester C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives only two singlets in its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, as shown. Which structure is it?
h: Two choices give a 9H singlet and a 3H singlet. Which CH<sub>3</sub> is on O (3.3–4.2 ppm) and which is next to C=O (≈2 ppm)?
w: A 9H singlet (t-Bu) and a 3H singlet. The 3H singlet at 3.66 ppm is an O–CH3, and the t-Bu at 1.20 ppm is on the carbonyl side. Methyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate, (CH3)3CCO2CH3.
x: tert-Butyl acetate also gives two singlets (9H, 3H), but its CH<sub>3</sub> is next to C=O (≈2.0 ppm) and its t-Bu is on O (≈1.45 ppm); no peak near 3.7.
Isobutyl acetate gives four signals: OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet, acetyl singlet, CH multiplet and 6H doublet.
Ethyl butanoate shows two ethyl-type patterns (quartet, triplets, sextet), not just singlets.

q: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of ethanol in CDCl<sub>3</sub> is shown. A drop of D<sub>2</sub>O is added and the tube is shaken. What change is seen?
c: The broad singlet near 2.6 ppm disappears; the rest are unchanged.
The quartet at 3.69 ppm becomes a triplet; the other signals stay the same.
The triplet at 1.22 ppm disappears; the other signals stay the same.
The broad singlet near 2.6 ppm becomes a triplet from coupling to the CH<sub>2</sub>.
h: Which H in ethanol is acidic enough to swap with deuterium? Deuterium does not appear in a <sup>1</sup>H spectrum.
w: The O–H proton exchanges with D2O (ROH + D2O ⇌ ROD + HOD), and O–D gives no 1H signal, so the broad OH singlet disappears. The CH2 quartet was never split by the OH (fast exchange already removed that coupling), so it stays a quartet.
x: The CH<sub>2</sub> was not coupled to the OH in the first place (fast exchange), so removing the OH H does not change its quartet.
C–H hydrogens do not exchange with D<sub>2</sub>O; only the O–H proton does.
The OH becomes OD, which has no <sup>1</sup>H signal at all; it cannot become a triplet.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give a 2H signal near δ 2.3?
h: Allylic H (on a carbon next to C=C) appear near 1.6–2.4 ppm; vinyl H at 4.5–6.5; H on O-bearing carbons at 3.3–4.2.
w: a =CH2 ≈ 5.0, b =CH ≈ 5.8, c allylic CH2 ≈ 2.3, d OCH2 ≈ 3.4 ppm. The 2H signal near 2.3 ppm is the allylic CH2, c.
x: H a are terminal vinyl H, near 5.0 ppm.
H b is a single vinyl H (1H) near 5.8 ppm.
H d are on a carbon bonded to O, near 3.4 ppm.

q: A <sup>13</sup>C NMR signal at δ 208 ppm most likely comes from which kind of carbon?
c: An sp<sup>3</sup> carbon bonded to O
h: Recall the <sup>13</sup>C regions: sp<sup>3</sup> C 0–50, C–O 50–90, C=C 100–150, ester/acid C=O 160–185, ketone/aldehyde C=O 190–220.
w: Ketone and aldehyde carbonyl carbons appear at 190–220 ppm. A signal at 208 ppm is a ketone C=O.
x: Ester C=O carbons are shielded by the extra O lone pair donation and appear near 165–175 ppm.
Alkene carbons appear at roughly 100–150 ppm.
sp<sup>3</sup> carbons bonded to O (alcohols, ethers) appear at about 50–90 ppm.

q: How does the tagged CH2 (a) of 2-butanone appear in the 1H NMR spectrum?
h: Neighbors are H on adjacent carbons only. Does the carbonyl carbon carry any H?
w: C2 is the C=O carbon and carries no H, so the CH2 couples only to the 3 H on C4: n + 1 = 4, a quartet, 2H. Being α to the C=O, it appears near 2.4 ppm.
x: A sextet counts the acetyl CH<sub>3</sub> as a neighbor, but it is on the far side of the C=O carbon (4 bonds away) and does not split the CH<sub>2</sub>.
A triplet would mean 2 neighbors; the adjacent carbon is a CH<sub>3</sub> with 3 H.
3.6 ppm is typical of a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to O; a CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O appears at 2–2.6 ppm.

q: Which C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Only two signals, 4H : 2H. Which isomer has two equivalent CH<sub>2</sub>Cl groups?
w: A 4H triplet at 3.70 ppm (two equivalent CH2Cl, each next to a CH2) and a 2H quintet at 2.21 ppm (the middle CH2, with 4 neighbors). 1,3-Dichloropropane, ClCH2CH2CH2Cl.
x: 1,2-Dichloropropane gives three signal groups: a CHCl multiplet (1H), a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (2H) and a 3H doublet near 1.6 ppm.
1,1-Dichloropropane shows a CHCl<sub>2</sub> triplet near 5.8 ppm (1H), a CH<sub>2</sub> multiplet and a 3H triplet.
2,2-Dichloropropane gives a single 6H singlet near 2.2 ppm.

q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown (DEPT results over the peaks). All four choices give three <sup>13</sup>C signals. Which one is it?
h: DBE = 2. Ask what the 127 ppm peak is (sp or sp<sup>2</sup>, and how many H), and what the two upfield CH<sub>2</sub> signals require.
w: The only low-field peak (127.3) is an sp2 CH; there are no other sp2 or sp carbons, so there is just one C=C, and DBE = 2 requires a ring. Two kinds of sp3 CH2 and no CH3: cyclohexene (C1/C2, C3/C6, C4/C5).
x: 3-Hexyne has sp carbons near 81 ppm with no H (DEPT: absent, quaternary) and a CH<sub>3</sub> signal; no sp<sup>2</sup> CH.
1,5-Hexadiene shows two sp<sup>2</sup> peaks (≈138 CH and ≈115 CH<sub>2</sub>) and only one sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>.
(E,E)-2,4-Hexadiene has two sp2 CH peaks and a CH3 near 18 ppm; it has no CH2.

q: Which C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Nothing appears between 3 and 4.5 ppm. What does that say about the carbon bearing Cl?
w: No signal near 3.4–4 ppm means the C–Cl carbon has no H: a tertiary chloride. A 6H singlet (two CH3 on the C–Cl carbon) plus an ethyl group (2H quartet, 3H triplet): 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.
x: 1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane has a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl singlet near 3.4 ppm and a 9H singlet; no ethyl pattern.
2-Chloro-3-methylbutane has a CHCl near 3.9 ppm (1H) and two different CH<sub>3</sub> doublets.
3-Chloropentane has a CHCl near 3.8 ppm (1H) and a 6H triplet; no 6H singlet.

q: Which chloroalkane gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: The 1H signal is a triplet and the 2H signal is a doublet: how many neighbors does each set have?
w: A 1H triplet (2 neighbors) at 5.77 ppm, deshielded by two Cl (CHCl2), and a 2H doublet (1 neighbor) at 3.96 ppm (CH2Cl). Cl2CH–CH2Cl, 1,1,2-trichloroethane.
x: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane has only a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet (3H) near 2.7 ppm.
1,2-Dichloroethane has four equivalent H: one singlet near 3.7 ppm.
1,1-Dichloroethane gives a 1H quartet (≈5.9) and a 3H doublet (≈2.1), the reverse multiplicities and a different ratio.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 4-ethyltoluene (shown)? Assume the aromatic H that are not related by symmetry give separate signals.
h: The para-disubstituted ring has a mirror plane through C1 and C4. How many kinds of ring H does that leave?
w: Ring H: two ortho to CH3 (equivalent pair) and two ortho to the ethyl (equivalent pair) = 2 signals (they appear as two doublets). Plus Ar–CH3 (s), CH2 (q) and the ethyl CH3 (t) = 5 signals.
x: Four treats all four ring H as one set; the H next to CH<sub>3</sub> and the H next to ethyl are different.
Six would need one more set; the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are already counted separately and the ring has only two kinds of H.
Seven counts each ring H separately, ignoring the mirror plane that makes them pairwise equivalent.

q:
Which pairs of compounds can be distinguished by the number of signals in their 13C NMR spectra alone?
I. cyclohexane and methylcyclopentane
II. 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane
III. pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane
h: Count the <sup>13</sup>C signals for each of the six compounds. A pair is distinguished only if the counts differ.
w: I: cyclohexane 1 signal, methylcyclopentane 4 → different. II: 1-chlorobutane 4, 2-chlorobutane 4 → same count (shifts differ, but the count does not). III: pentane 3 (C1/C5, C2/C4, C3), 2,2-dimethylpropane 2 → different. I and III only.
x: Pair III is also distinguished: pentane gives 3 signals and 2,2-dimethylpropane gives 2.
Pair II gives the same count (4 and 4), while pair I is distinguished (1 vs 4 signals).
Pair II fails: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane each give 4 signals.

q: An ester C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR data below, with raw integral areas. How many hydrogens does the δ 0.93 signal represent?
h: Add the areas, divide by the total number of H, then divide each area by that value.
w: Total area = 21.0 + 31.6 + 10.4 + 63.0 = 126.0 for 12 H, or 10.5 per H. The signals are 2H, 3H, 1H and 63.0/10.5 = 6H. (This fits isobutyl acetate: OCH2 d, CH3C=O s, CH m, (CH3)2 d.)
x: 3H assumes the 0.93 signal is one CH<sub>3</sub>, but its area is twice that of the 3H singlet at 2.05 ppm (63.0 vs 31.6), so it is 6H.
9H would require 63.0 to be 75% of the total area, but it is 50% (63.0 of 126.0).
4H does not match any whole-number ratio of the areas; 63.0/10.5 = 6.

q: Which alkane gives exactly three signals in its 1H NMR spectrum?
h: For each structure, group the H into equivalent sets (same carbon type, related by symmetry).
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane, (CH3)3C–CH2CH3: the t-Bu methyls (9H, s), the CH2 (2H, q) and the CH3 (3H, t). Three signals.
x: 2-Methylbutane has 4 sets: two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> (6H), CH, CH<sub>2</sub> and the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub>.
2,3-Dimethylbutane is highly symmetric: four equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> and two equivalent CH give only 2 signals.
2,2,4-Trimethylpentane has 4 sets: t-Bu (9H), CH<sub>2</sub>, CH and two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> (6H).

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR data below. Its IR spectrum has no O–H band. Which structure is it?
h: DBE = 1. Is there any carbon above 100 ppm? If not, where does the degree of unsaturation go?
w: DBE = 1, but no 13C peak above 100 ppm, so there is no C=O or C=C: the unsaturation is a ring. Only two carbon environments (67.9, C–O; 25.7) and two 4H signals mean a symmetric ring with two OCH2 and two CH2: tetrahydrofuran.
x: 2-Butanone has a C=O carbon near 209 ppm and four <sup>13</sup>C signals.
Ethyl vinyl ether has two sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (≈150 and ≈87 ppm) and vinyl H at 4–6.5 ppm.
3-Buten-1-ol has sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (≈135, 117 ppm), vinyl H and an O–H (IR ≈3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>).

q: The H of a terminal alkyne (≈2 ppm) appears well upfield of a vinyl H (4.5–6.5 ppm). Why?
c: Circulation of the cylindrical π electrons around the C≡C axis creates a local field that shields the alkyne H.
The sp carbon is less electronegative than an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, so the C–H bond is more electron-rich.
The alkyne H exchanges rapidly with the solvent, which moves its signal upfield.
The alkyne H has no neighbors to couple with, and uncoupled H appear upfield.
h: Think about magnetic anisotropy: where does the induced field of the π cloud reinforce or oppose the applied field?
w: The applied field drives the π electrons of a triple bond to circulate around the bond axis. The induced field opposes the applied field along the axis, exactly where the alkyne H sits, so the H is shielded by the induced π-electron field. In an alkene the H lies in the deshielding region of the π circulation.
x: The trend runs the other way: an sp carbon (50% s character) is more electronegative than sp<sup>2</sup>, which by itself would deshield the H.
Terminal alkyne C–H does not exchange quickly with CDCl<sub>3</sub>; exchange affects O–H and N–H protons.
Coupling changes the splitting of a signal, not its chemical shift.
